title: School Bus–Sized Octopuses Ruled the Dino Seas!
summary: Have you ever heard of the kraken, a giant sea monster from old stories? Well, scientists just found proof that a real-life giant octopus once swam in our oceans—and it was as big as a school bus! Back when dinosaurs walked on land, these huge octopuses ruled the seas. They were the biggest animals without backbones ever known. Scientists call them Nanaimoteuthis haggarti (say: Nuh-NY-moh-TOOTH-is Ha-GAR-tee). How do we know they existed? Octopuses are soft and squishy, so they rarely turn into fossils. But they have a hard, beak-like jaw made of a tough material called chitin (KY-tin). That jaw can survive and become a fossil. A team of scientists studied 15 fossil jaws found in Japan and Canada. Some jaws were still stuck in rocks, so they used a special 3-D scanning trick to see inside without breaking them. By comparing the jaws to modern octopus and squid jaws, they figured out how big the ancient ones were. The largest jaw could hold a grapefruit—and was half again as big as a modern giant squid's jaw! The ancient octopus could stretch 23 to 63 feet from head to arm tips. That's longer than an ambulance! These giants were early finned octopuses, like today's cute dumbo octopus, but way bigger. Scratches on the jaws show they were fierce hunters, crunching shells and bones. They may have even competed with giant sea reptiles for food. Next time you see an octopus at the aquarium, remember its school bus–sized cousin that once ruled the deep!
why_it_matters: Discovering this giant octopus shows that even soft, squishy creatures can leave behind clues from millions of years ago, inspiring us to imagine what other mysterious animals might be hiding in the fossil record - or even alive deep in the ocean today.

background_read: During the age of dinosaurs, the oceans were filled with giant marine reptiles like plesiosaurs and mosasaurs. Huge predators competed for food, and this newly discovered giant octopus was likely one of the top hunters.

The fossils were found in Japan and Canada, which shows that this enormous octopus lived across the Pacific Ocean around 80 million years ago. Its modern cousin, the dumbo octopus (a tiny deep-sea octopus with ear-like fins), is just a fraction of its size.
Article_Structure: WHAT: Proof of a school bus–sized ancient octopus, Nanaimoteuthis haggarti
WHERE: Fossil remains found in Japan and Canada; the creature lived in ancient oceans worldwide
WHY: To learn about the size and hunting habits of soft-bodied prehistoric predators that rarely leave fossils

perspectives.description: This find fills an important gap in our knowledge. Finding proof of such a huge octopus helps us understand how backboneless animals could grow to enormous sizes and dominate the seas alongside giant reptiles.

Because only the hard beak was fossilized, we still don't know exactly what the rest of the octopus looked like. The size estimates are based on comparisons with modern squids, so there may be more to discover.
Using 3-D scanning allowed scientists to see inside fossil rocks without damaging them, a method that opens up new ways to study delicate remains from extinct animals all over the world.
